common_name: Blue Boy African Violet (Historic Original 1927 Purple-Blue Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Blue Boy was one of the very first African violet cultivars introduced into American commerce in the late 1920s.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Blue Boy bears single, deep purple-blue flowers over a neat rosette of fuzzy, dark green leaves, and holds a special place in horticultural history as one of the earliest African violet cultivars sold commercially in the United States, helping launch the enormous wave of popularity the species has enjoyed as a houseplant ever since. Though simpler in form than many modern ruffled, double, or fantasy-patterned cultivars, its historic significance keeps it in circulation among African violet collectors and society show entries. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, water carefully to avoid wetting the crown and leaves, and rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

common_name: Pip Squeek African Violet (Micro-Miniature African Violet)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Pip Squeek is a micro-miniature cultivar staying only a few inches across at full maturity.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Pip Squeek is a micro-miniature African violet, staying only a few inches across at full maturity, with small pink-and-white flowers held over a tiny, tightly formed rosette proportional to the plant's diminutive scale. Its small size makes it a favorite for thimble pots, terrariums, and collector displays where dozens of miniature violets can be grown in the space a single standard-sized plant would need. Water very carefully with a micro-miniature this small, since overwatering is even more damaging at this scale, and feed at a diluted strength appropriate for tiny root systems. Rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

common_name: Powwow African Violet (White Fantasy-Patterned Blue-Flecked Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Powwow is a fantasy-patterned cultivar, a category prized for irregular flecks and streaks of contrasting color on each flower.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Powwow bears white flowers speckled and streaked with blue-purple fantasy markings, a mottled, no-two-alike pattern belonging to the fantasy class of African violet cultivars that collectors prize precisely because each flush of bloom can show slightly different patterning on the same plant. Its patterned flowers stand out clearly against the dark green foliage rosette in a mixed collection of African violets. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, water carefully to avoid wetting the crown and leaves, and rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

common_name: Fancy Pants African Violet (Ruffled Bicolor Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Fancy Pants is grown for its heavily ruffled, bicolor flower form.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Fancy Pants bears large, heavily ruffled, bicolor flowers combining two contrasting shades in each bloom, the frilled, wavy petal edges giving the flowers a fuller, more elaborate look than a plain single-form African violet. Its showy, ruffled blooms make it a popular choice for African violet society show entries as well as home collections. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, water carefully to avoid wetting the crown and leaves, and rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

common_name: Buckeye Seduction African Violet (Deep Red Ruffled Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Part of the prolific Buckeye breeding line of modern African violet cultivars developed in Ohio.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Buckeye Seduction bears large, ruffled, deep red flowers over a full rosette of dark green foliage, part of the extensive Buckeye line of African violet cultivars bred by hybridizer Ralph Robinson, a breeding program responsible for hundreds of modern named cultivars prized in collector and show circles for vigorous growth and richly saturated flower color. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, water carefully to avoid wetting the crown and leaves, and rotate the pot periodically for even, symmetrical growth toward the light source.

common_name: Wrangler's Ricochet African Violet (Trailing Miniature Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. A trailing-habit cultivar from the Wrangler breeding line, part of a category of African violets that branch and spread rather than forming a single rosette.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix. Wrangler's Ricochet branches from multiple crowns to form a spreading, trailing plant rather than the single tidy rosette typical of standard African violets, making it better suited to a hanging pot or a shallow, wide container where its cascading habit can be shown off. Like other trailing types it needs less frequent grooming of side shoots than a standard violet, since multiple crowns are part of its intended growth habit rather than a fault to correct. Feed every four weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets, water carefully to avoid wetting the crown and leaves, and give a wide, shallow pot room to spread.
